name: PT Olympus Strategic Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Olympus Strategic Indonesia: a Bali hotel shell recast as a coal holding, priced for perfection
frontmatter.summary: A Bali villa developer became a coal holding company in early 2026 through a nominally priced related-party acquisition of Orbit Marketing and its consolidated Terracom coal business. The first consolidated quarter lost money at the gross-profit line and the shares trade at several times book. We initiate at SELL.
thesis: The company is no longer a lodging name. Coal revenue is now the overwhelming majority of group sales, so the Yahoo sector label and the industry template understate cyclical and asset-quality risk.
The first consolidated quarter shows cost of revenue above revenue, a negative gross margin, and an operating cash inflow driven by an unexplained other operating receipt rather than by operations.
A controlling shareholder bought in at a small fraction of today's price, then injected the operating business for nominal consideration, creating a large non-cash equity reserve.

Our base-case DCF values the group well below the market price even after assuming coal margins normalise to a thin thermal level and crediting the parent's ownership share of the equity-method investments, the net cash and the coal enterprise value on one consistent rule.
The shares are a finite-reserve, loss-making coal producer with a tiny hotel portfolio and no dividend history; we see no valuation support between here and book value.

catalysts.event: Q3 2026 consolidated results, the second full quarter of coal consolidation
FY2026 audited accounts, first full-year consolidation and purchase-price allocation
Any further related-party acquisition or asset injection by the controlling shareholder

blocks.text: **Rating SELL; target Rp210 against a last price of Rp1,000, an expected return of -79.0%.**

This is not the company its sector label says it is. PT Olympus Strategic Indonesia Tbk was formerly PT Surya Permata Andalan Tbk, a Bali villa and hotel developer whose portfolio was limited to a handful of small properties [S4]. Between the December 2025 change of control and the January 2026 acquisition of Orbit Marketing Pte. Ltd., the listed vehicle was transformed into a coal-focused holding company: its first consolidated quarter reports coal revenue of IDR337.8bn against hotel revenue of IDR3.4bn [S5]. We initiate coverage at SELL because the economics of the acquired business do not support the price, and because the structure of the transaction leaves minority holders exposed to a controlling shareholder whose interests and entry price are very different from theirs.

The variant view is simple. The market appears to price the shares on the story of a new controlling shareholder and a coal asset, at a market capitalisation of Rp8,001,111,504,000 and a price that has more than doubled over the year, having traded as high as Rp1,265 [S0]. Our work prices the cash flows. In the first consolidated quarter, cost of revenue exceeded revenue, giving a negative gross margin, and the group booked a loss before tax [S5]. Our base case holds the first quarter's economics for the stub and then allows only a break-even mine gate and a thin thermal margin, and it still produces a value of Rp135 per share, an order of magnitude below today's price. The bear case, in which the coal business stays at the debut-quarter economics and the rehabilitation provision is drawn, is worth Rp0. The bull case, which requires a normal thermal-coal margin and a recovery in the hotels, reaches Rp597 and is still not enough to justify the current quote.

What moves the value is therefore narrow and identifiable. First, the realised coal price against the group's mining and logistics cost base, which today is inverted. Second, the treatment of the large non-cash equity reserve and the related-party acquisition price, which determine whether reported book value is real or an accounting artefact. Third, the hotel assets, which are small in revenue terms but carry the only genuinely owned property in the group. We discuss each in turn, and we set out in the risk section exactly which assumptions the red team should attack.
What the company does now

PT Olympus Strategic Indonesia Tbk describes its activities as development, services, trade and investment, and states that the business currently carried on is management services and investment in subsidiaries [S5]. That description no longer captures the group. Following the acquisition of Orbit Marketing Pte. Ltd. through Quantum Strategic Investments Pte. Ltd. in January 2026, the consolidated group derives most of its revenue from coal, with hotel operations a small residual [S5]. The accounting policy note is explicit that revenue from contracts with customers is generally derived from coal revenue and from the sale of goods and services in the hotel and management businesses [S5]. Coal revenue in the first consolidated quarter was IDR337.8bn; hotel revenue was IDR3.4bn [S5].

The coal business is conducted through Terracom Limited, an Australian-domiciled entity in which the group holds an indirect 45.8% interest but which is consolidated as a subsidiary [S5]. That ownership structure matters: the non-controlling interest absorbed slightly more than half of the first-quarter group loss, and the minority position on the balance sheet is negative, reflecting net liabilities inside the coal subsidiary [S5]. The balance sheet also carries equity-method investments of IDR980.6bn, restricted cash of IDR634.2bn, and long-term provisions of IDR779.9bn, which we read as mine rehabilitation and related obligations [S5]. In other words, the group is an operating coal consolidator with a large rehabilitation liability, not a property company with a coal option.
The hotel portfolio

The legacy business operates three small properties through subsidiaries: Chill Hotel Seminyak, Chandi Hotel Ubud and Alami Luxury Villa Seminyak [S4]. The annual report describes a strategy built on digital marketing and online travel agents to lift occupancy, and on destination diversification [S4]. The hotel segment generated IDR3.4bn of revenue in the first quarter, broadly flat on the prior-year period [S5]. The properties sit inside a group whose property, plant and equipment was IDR1,502.9bn at 31 March 2026, after the acquisition added the mine assets, and whose land is carried at cost, so the hotels are a genuine but small asset within a much larger coal balance sheet [S5]. We treat them as a separately valued stub rather than as the core of the investment case.
Group structure and control

The controlling shareholder is PT Mercury Strategic Indonesia, which acquired 26.9% of the company in a negotiated transaction in December 2025 at a price of Rp183 per share [S3]. A second holder, PT Sukses Makmur Jayapratama, held 603.7m shares at 31 March 2026, down from 853.7m at 31 December 2025, a sale of a third of its holding in the quarter the coal business was injected, and the public holds the rest [S5]. The December purchase price is a useful anchor: the controlling shareholder bought control at a small fraction of the current market price, and the subsequent injection of the operating business at nominal consideration creates a large gap between their economic entry and that of a buyer today [S3][S5].
Strategy and footprint

The strategy that emerges from the filings is a roll-up: a listed shell, a new controlling shareholder, an acquisition of a Singapore investment vehicle holding a coal business, and the retention of the legacy Bali hotels. No volume, reserve or production guidance has been published for the coal operations in the materials available to us, and no mine plan or offtake contract is disclosed [S5]. That absence is itself a finding: we cannot underwrite volumes, strip ratios or reserve life, so our model is revenue-driven and calibrated to the first consolidated quarter rather than to a physical mine plan.

Indonesian listed shells are occasionally used as acquisition vehicles by new controlling shareholders. The economics of such a transaction depend less on the operating business than on the price at which the new assets are injected and on whether minority holders share in the value created. Where an asset is injected at a nominal price, the accounting gain appears as an equity reserve rather than as cash, so reported book value can rise sharply without any cash entering the company.
The relevant industry is thermal coal, not lodging

The company's Yahoo sector classification is consumer cyclical and its industry is lodging [S0]. That classification was correct for the legacy business and is now misleading. In the first consolidated quarter, coal accounted for the overwhelming majority of revenue [S5]. We therefore analyse the company against thermal-coal economics, while retaining the leisure and tourism template only because the desk and configuration require it. The mismatch is material and should be corrected at the next classification review.

The macro desk's current stance on thermal coal is neutral, in a balance-of-payments-pressure regime in which rate-sensitive domestic consumer names are avoided [BRIEF]. We do not import any commodity price forecast into the model: the assumptions in this report are revenue and margin based, and the coal price deck is not used because the group does not disclose the calorific grade, the sales destination or the index against which its coal is priced [S5]. That is a genuine evidence gap, and we flag it rather than fill it.
Scale, cost position and the first-quarter evidence

The group's coal operation is small. Quarterly coal revenue of IDR337.8bn is a modest absolute number for an Indonesian producer, and the cost structure reported in the notes is unfavourable: mining and processing cost of IDR355.0bn and selling and marketing cost of IDR124.4bn against that revenue [S5]. Mining and processing alone exceeded coal revenue, which means the operation was, on the reported numbers, selling coal below its direct extraction cost before logistics. That is either a temporary distortion of the acquisition quarter, a grade and quality problem, or a transfer-pricing outcome inside a related-party structure. The filings do not let us distinguish between those explanations, and we treat the ambiguity as a core risk rather than resolving it in the company's favour.
Competitive position

There is no disclosed market share, no reserve statement and no production figure in the materials we reviewed [S5]. On any reasonable reading, a producer of this size is a price-taker with no influence over the thermal-coal benchmark, no visible cost advantage, and no moat. The hotel assets are small independent properties in Bali, a market with abundant supply and a highly cyclical demand base [S4]. The group's only structural advantage is access to a listed vehicle and a controlling shareholder willing to inject assets; that is a financing advantage, not an operating one.
Five forces

Supplier power is high: mining services, fuel, logistics and port capacity are concentrated and the group has no disclosed long-term contracts. Buyer power is high: coal is a commodity and the buyer can switch at the benchmark price. The threat of new entrants is moderate globally but low at the margin where this producer sits. Substitution is a long-run structural threat as the energy transition reduces thermal-coal demand. Rivalry is intense among Indonesian producers, many of which are larger and lower cost. The one force that cuts in the company's favour is the scarcity of listed coal vehicles, which explains the share-price behaviour but does not create operating value [S5][S4].
Regulation

Indonesian coal mining is governed by the mining licence regime, with royalty rates that depend on licence type and calorific value, and with domestic market obligations. The filings do not disclose the licence type, the royalty rate actually paid, or the domestic sales obligation for the consolidated operation [S5]. We therefore cannot calibrate a royalty schedule, and our model treats royalty as part of the reported cost base rather than as a separate, licence-driven line. This is a limitation the red team should note: a formal royalty schedule could move the valuation, in either direction, once the licence is disclosed.

Thermal-coal producers in Indonesia sell at a discount or premium to the benchmark depending on calorific value, ash, sulphur and moisture. Logistics and barging can absorb a large share of the mine-gate price for producers far from a port. Licence type determines the royalty formula, and a change in the licence regime can alter the economics of a marginal mine more than a movement in the coal price itself.
History: a small hotel business until the acquisition

The reported history is that of the legacy hotel company. Revenue rose from IDR4.9bn in FY2022A to IDR16.7bn in FY2025A, with a gross margin that was healthy on the small base but an operating result that barely broke even [S0]. The group paid no dividend in any year of the price history [S0]. The data pack depreciation line is materially understated: the FY2025 audited depreciation charge is IDR2.5bn, several times the figure in the pack, because the direct-method cash-flow presentation obscures the real charge [S4]. We have restated FY2025 depreciation from the audited filing, and that restatement rebuilds the historical EBITDA line.

| | FY2022A | FY2023A | FY2024A | FY2025A | |---|---|---|---|---| | Revenue | IDR4.9bn | IDR12.5bn | IDR17.9bn | IDR16.7bn | | Gross profit | IDR2.8bn | IDR7.4bn | IDR10.2bn | IDR9.9bn | | EBITDA | IDR-2.9bn | IDR0.7bn | IDR2.2bn | IDR2.9bn | | Net profit to parent | IDR-1.3bn | IDR0.7bn | IDR1.2bn | IDR0.1bn |
The first consolidated quarter

The March 2026 quarter is the first to consolidate the coal business, and it is the single most important piece of evidence in this report. Revenue was IDR341.1bn, cost of revenue was IDR536.6bn, and the result was a gross loss [S5]. Mining and processing cost of IDR355.0bn and selling and marketing cost of IDR124.4bn together explain almost the whole of the cost line [S5]. Depreciation, including the charge embedded in cost of revenue, was IDR52.6bn for the quarter, a very heavy charge against the acquired asset base [S5]. The reported loss before tax was negative, and the parent's share was smaller than the group loss because the non-controlling interest took the majority [S5].

Two features of the cash-flow statement deserve scrutiny. First, operating cash flow was strongly positive, but the direct-method statement shows that the inflow was driven by an other operating income receipt of IDR643.5bn, against only a small positive other-income line in the profit and loss account [S5]. That is not trading cash generation; it is an unexplained inflow that we cannot tie to the operations, and until the company explains it we treat it as non-recurring. Second, the statement records a cash outflow for the acquisition of subsidiaries of IDR594.3bn, which is difficult to reconcile with the nominal stated purchase price for the shares of Orbit Marketing [S5]. The difference may be cash that moved with the acquired entity, a subscription into the vehicle, or a related-party payment; the filing does not say. Both items are earnings-quality flags of the optical, if not manipulation, class, and we would need the notes to the next set of accounts before relying on either.
Our forecast

We model FY2026E revenue of IDR1,646.3bn, which is the annualised run-rate of the coal business as consolidated from the acquisition date plus the hotel stub [S5]. Growth then settles at a low single-digit rate, because no volume growth plan, reserve expansion or new mine is disclosed [S5]. Gross margin is the pivotal assumption: we assume -12.0% for FY2026E, a blend of the loss-making first quarter and a normalising remainder of the year, rising to a thin thermal margin by the end of the forecast [S5]. Operating costs fall from 9.0% of revenue to 7.0% as integration costs lapse. Depreciation stays high at 8.0% of revenue, reflecting the acquired asset base. Capex is assumed at 4.0% of revenue for maintenance only, since no development plan is disclosed. Working capital is modelled flat: incremental working capital is held at 0.0% of revenue and we take no cash release from the negative balance at the acquisition date.

The resulting forecast still shows a loss at the operating line in FY2026E, of IDR-345.7bn, with operating profit turning positive only in FY2029E [model]. The parent's share of the loss is cushioned by the minority, but that cushion is accounting, not economics: the minority share of the subsidiary losses is a claim that grows as the subsidiary deteriorates [S5]. We do not book the acquisition-date payables as a release, because the negative working-capital position at 31 March 2026 is a level, not a recurring source of cash [S5]. We tax the coal entity at the Australian statutory rate from FY2029E, once the accumulated deficit is absorbed, rather than assuming a tax-free decade [S5]. We do not assume a dividend at any point in the forecast, consistent with the group record and its accumulated deficit [S5].
Balance sheet and debt

At 31 March 2026 the group reported cash of IDR529.6bn, restricted cash of IDR634.2bn, lease liabilities of IDR117.0bn, trade payables of IDR502.2bn, other payables of IDR596.1bn, long-term provisions of IDR779.9bn, and equity attributable to the parent of IDR2,093.0bn [S5]. There are no bank borrowings disclosed. The reported equity includes a non-cash other equity reserve of IDR1,376.6bn created on the acquisition, which is why book value jumped without a corresponding cash inflow [S5]. Our engine rolling equity line does not capture that reserve, so the forecast balance sheet understates reported group equity; the reader should use the March 2026 filing for the actual position and treat the forecast equity line as a modelling construct [S5].

The liquidity picture is better than the income statement suggests only because of the restricted cash and the acquisition inflow. Trade and other payables together exceed cash, and the rehabilitation provision is large relative to the asset base [S5]. A coal business with negative margins and a rehabilitation liability is a cash consumer over its life, and the equity cushion is thinner than the headline book value implies.
Earnings-quality flags

Our screen raises four flags. The accruals picture is extreme and in the opposite direction to the usual warning: net profit is negative while operating cash flow is strongly positive, but the cash flow is driven by the unexplained other operating receipt and a large payables build rather than by collections [S5]. Receivables scale with the new coal revenue and cannot be compared with the legacy history. Related-party gravity is high: the controlling shareholder bought in at a negotiated price and the operating business was injected through a vehicle it controls [S3][S5]. Structure flags include a nominal-price acquisition, a large non-cash equity reserve, and a negative minority interest [S5]. We classify the accounting items as optics-class pending the notes, and the related-party items as a structural discount rather than a proven manipulation.
Method choice

We use a discounted cash flow as the primary method because the company owns a finite coal asset and a small property portfolio, and because earnings multiples are unusable: the group is loss-making, so the price-to-earnings method is dropped by the engine, and the EV/EBITDA cross-check was dropped on the same basis, because it applied a leisure peer median multiple to a negative consolidated EBITDA and produced a floored zero that carried a fifth of the target by construction. The DCF now carries the whole weight [model].

The discount rate is built from an Indonesian risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, a country risk premium of 2.5%, and a levered beta of 0.91, giving a cost of equity of 11.9% and a WACC of 11.9% [model]. One step in that build is easy to miss: the quoted risk-free rate is reduced by a 1.6% sovereign default spread before it enters the formula, because the rupiah yield embeds a default premium that the country risk premium would otherwise double-count, so the cost of equity is the net rate plus the levered beta times the mature premium plus the country premium. Without the deduction the inputs would sum to a higher cost of equity and a lower value. The beta is the industry default and we regard it as too low for a marginal coal producer; a higher beta would lower the value. The WACC sits at the bottom of the house band for Indonesian rupiah assets, so our valuation is, if anything, generous on the discount rate.
The DCF

The base-case DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR705.4bn and an equity value of Rp120 per share, with terminal value accounting for 70.5% of the total [model]. The bridge applies one ownership rule to every consolidated item. The DCF consolidates the whole of the coal cash flows although the group holds only 45.8% of Terracom, acquired through Orbit Marketing, so the enterprise value is reduced by the minority's remaining share of it. The IDR980.6bn of equity-method investments sits inside that same subsidiary, so only the parent's share of the carrying value is credited; the remainder is deducted. The net cash arrived with the same acquisition, so the same split is applied to it rather than crediting the parent with cash the minority owns; the bridge line shows the amount, and retaining the whole balance would add it straight back to equity value. The negative minority book value is no longer added back, because the market-value claims above replace it [S5]. On this bridge the parent claims Rp120 per share.

The target in this version is lower than in the first draft: the minority's share of the net cash is now deducted alongside its share of the enterprise value and the associates, where the earlier bridge credited that cash in full. The correction runs through all three scenarios, not just the base case.

The multiple-survival test points the opposite way to the one we first wrote, and the correction matters for how the short is framed. The terminal value capitalises FY2035E EBITDA of IDR240.9bn at a low single-digit exit multiple, which is far below the multiple the market already pays on much earlier earnings: today's enterprise value is 70.9x FY2028E EBITDA, years before the terminal year [model]. So our DCF is not leaning on a rich exit; its exit is conservative, and the value it produces still sits far under the price. The short does not rest on the exit multiple at all. It rests on the entry: the market is paying a decade-ahead multiple today for a business that lost money at the gross-profit line in its first consolidated quarter.
Cross-checks and what the price implies

The market capitalisation is Rp8,001,111,504,000 against book value attributable to the parent of IDR2,093.0bn at the last balance-sheet date [S0][S5]. The shares therefore trade at a large multiple of the only hard asset value in the filing, for a business that lost money at the gross-profit line in its first consolidated quarter. The EV/EBITDA cross-check was dropped rather than shown: a leisure peer median applied to negative coal EBITDA produces a floored zero that would silently cut the target by a fifth, which is not a valuation [model].

The reverse DCF asks what growth the current price requires. On our margin assumptions, today's price implies FY2027E revenue growth of 35.8% against our base case of 4.0% [model]. That gap is the valuation case in one number: the market is paying for a growth trajectory the filings do not support.
Sensitivity

The value is most sensitive to the coal gross margin, then to the discount rate, then to the terminal growth rate. A one-point change in the gross margin moves the value by more than the entire hotel segment revenue, which is why we do not present the hotels as a support. The sensitivity table sets out the grid.
Sum-of-the-parts cross-check

As a sanity check, we value the parts. The hotels are a small, stable, asset-backed business; at a modest multiple of their revenue they are worth a small fraction of the market capitalisation. The equity-method investments are carried at IDR980.6bn, but they sit inside the 45.8%-owned coal subsidiary, so the sum-of-the-parts credits the parent's share only, the same share the DCF bridge uses and the same figure it shows net of the minority deduction; taking the full carrying value here while deducting the minority in the DCF would count the same asset twice. Net cash is positive once the restricted cash is treated as unavailable and the lease liabilities are deducted, and it is split on the same ownership basis. The coal business, on our base case, is worth the present value of a thin margin over a finite life. Summing the parts does not reach the current price, which is consistent with the DCF. We do not publish a second precise sum-of-the-parts number because the disclosure does not let us split the balance sheet cleanly between coal and hotels [S5]; the parts and their ownership-adjusted contribution are in the DCF bridge table.
Downside risks

**Commodity and margin risk (high likelihood, high impact).** The first consolidated quarter had cost of revenue above revenue [S5]. If that is structural rather than a purchase-accounting artefact, the coal business destroys value every quarter, and the equity is worth little more than the sum of net cash and the equity-method investments.

**Related-party and structure risk (high likelihood, high impact).** The controlling shareholder acquired its stake at Rp183 per share in December 2025, and the operating business was injected at a nominal share price [S3][S5]. Minority holders have no visibility on future related-party transactions, and the large non-cash equity reserve is not cash. The change of control also triggers a mandatory tender offer to minorities, disclosed in the same announcement [S3]; no priced offer document has been archived, so we cannot test the tender price as a reference point and treat the absence as a disclosure gap rather than as support.

**Accounting and disclosure risk (medium likelihood, high impact).** The operating cash inflow of IDR643.5bn described as other operating income is not explained, and the IDR594.3bn acquisition outflow does not reconcile with the stated purchase price [S5]. Until the notes explain both, reported cash flow should not be relied upon.

**Rehabilitation and environmental risk (medium likelihood, high impact).** Long-term provisions of IDR779.9bn are large relative to the coal asset base, and the cost of mine closure could exceed the provision [S5].

**Liquidity and price risk (high likelihood, medium impact).** The shares have traded between Rp143 and Rp1,265 over the year, and the free float is 65.6% [S0]. A stock with this price history can move far from value for long periods, which is a risk to a short as much as to a long.

**Regulatory and licence risk (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The licence type, royalty rate and domestic market obligation of the coal operation are not disclosed [S5]. A less favourable licence regime would compress the margin further.

**FX risk (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Coal is priced in US dollars and the group reports in rupiah, so a stronger dollar helps revenue while raising imported cost; the macro desk regime is one of balance-of-payments pressure with rupiah risk [BRIEF].

**Governance risk (high likelihood, high impact).** A newly controlling shareholder, a nominal-price injection and a negative minority interest are the classic ingredients of value transfer away from minorities on IDX [S3][S5].
Scenarios

We mirror the bear and bull cases around the same drivers and keep the base case at the most probable outcome. The base case assumes the coal margin normalises to a thin thermal level; the bear case holds the debut-quarter economics; the bull case assumes a full thermal margin plus a hotel re-rating. Probabilities are 30.0%, 45.0% and 25.0%.

The bear case is worth Rp0, the base case Rp135 and the bull case Rp597. Even the bull case is below the current price, which is the cleanest statement of our view: the market is not paying for the bull case, it is paying for something beyond it.
What would change our view

A disclosed mine plan with reserves, volumes, strip ratio and cash cost would let us underwrite the coal business properly, and could move us to a constructive stance if the cost position proves better than the first quarter suggests. A clear explanation of the other operating income and the acquisition outflow would remove a large part of the governance discount. A credible, independently valued exit for the equity-method investments would support the book value. Conversely, a further related-party acquisition, a rights issue, or a rehabilitation drawdown would confirm the bear case.
Ownership and control

PT Mercury Strategic Indonesia holds 26.9% following the December 2025 negotiated purchase of a controlling block at Rp183 per share [S3]. PT Sukses Makmur Jayapratama and the public hold the remainder [S4]. The free float reported by the data pack is 65.6% and insider ownership 34.4% [S0]. The concentration of control in a single shareholder, combined with the nominal-price injection of the operating business, means minority holders are dependent on the controlling shareholder continued willingness to inject value rather than extract it.
Related parties and structure

The acquisition of Orbit Marketing through Quantum Strategic Investments, a group vehicle, is the defining related-party event [S5]. The stated share purchase price was nominal, while the cash-flow statement shows a much larger outflow described as acquisition of subsidiaries [S5]. The difference is unexplained in the materials we reviewed. We also note the negative non-controlling interest and the large other equity reserve, both of which arise from the same transaction [S5]. None of these is evidence of fraud; together they are a structure that requires a discount until explained.
Board and auditor

The board includes a president director and directors with hospitality and mining backgrounds, including a director who also sits on the board of the controlling shareholder [S4]. We have not been able to review the auditor opinion or any emphasis of matter in the materials fetched for this initiation, and we flag that as an open item for the revision. The company changed its name in February 2026, which is a routine consequence of the change of control but also complicates the comparability of the historical record [S5].
Dividends and capital allocation

No dividend has been paid in any year of the price history, and the group carries an accumulated deficit [S0][S5]. Capital allocation is therefore entirely at the discretion of the controlling shareholder, and the first use of cash after the acquisition was the acquisition itself. A rights issue to fund the coal business cannot be ruled out and would dilute per-share value.
ESG exposures

The group ESG exposure is now dominated by coal: mine safety, land rehabilitation, water and tailings management, and the energy transition. The annual report sustainability section still reads as a hotel document, discussing guest satisfaction and green hotels, which suggests the sustainability framework has not caught up with the business [S4]. The rehabilitation provision of IDR779.9bn is the most tangible ESG-related liability on the balance sheet [S5]. For a marginal producer, the cost of compliance is a fixed burden that a larger producer can spread over more tonnes.

The near-term catalysts are the Q3 2026 consolidated results, which will show whether the first-quarter gross loss was a one-off, and the FY2026 audited accounts, which will contain the purchase-price allocation and, we hope, the notes explaining the other operating income and the acquisition outflow [S5]. Any further related-party transaction by the controlling shareholder is a catalyst in either direction [S3].

The KPIs we watch are: the realised coal price against mining and processing cost per tonne, once volumes are disclosed; the gross margin, which is the single line that drives the valuation; the selling and marketing cost as a share of coal revenue; the rehabilitation provision against the asset base; the equity-method investments and any impairment; the cash and restricted cash split; and the share count, given the risk of a rights issue [S5]. We also watch the coal price deck and the rupiah, not because we forecast them, but because they set the range within which the margin can normalise [BRIEF].

Our monitoring stance is simple: we need the second and third consolidated quarters to confirm whether the debut quarter was an artefact [S5]. If it was, and if the coal margin settles at a normal thermal level, our base case is broadly right and the shares remain expensive. If it was not, the bear case is the base case and the downside is larger than our target implies.

S0.title: Yahoo Finance statements, prices and profile for NATO.JK

S3.title: Mercury Strategic is new controller of NATO, shares jump 24.51% | IDNFinancials

bear.narrative: Coal stays at or below the Q1 2026 economics (mining cost above the realised price, logistics at a third of revenue), the Rp779.9bn rehabilitation provision is drawn through operating cost as the mine moves to closure, the Rp980.6bn associates are impaired and the hotels absorb cash; margins never recover. With no separate provision or impairment line in the engine, the draw is expressed through the gross-margin and opex shocks, which is why they are wider than the bull's mirror.

bull.narrative: The acquisition stub was distorted and coal settles at a normal thermal margin with logistics renegotiated; the 45.84%-owned Terracom stake contributes fully and the hotels recover. The mirrored +15pp margin is the same distance above our base as the bear is below it; a further nominal-price injection is not valued because the one observed injection added a Rp779.9bn rehabilitation liability and a loss-making quarter, so its earnings accretion to minorities is negative.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E re-bases revenue onto the consolidated coal business: Q1 2026 coal revenue of Rp337.8bn was earned in about 2.5 months from the 16 January acquisition date, i.e. a ~Rp1.62tn annual run-rate plus ~Rp13bn of hotel revenue. Later years grow 3-4% on coal volume and price, not on further acquisitions (none announced).

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Q1 2026 is the only consolidated evidence: coal mining and processing cost of Rp355.0bn against coal revenue of Rp337.8bn (-5% at the mine gate) plus Rp124.4bn of selling and logistics (note 21), giving a -57% consolidated margin. FY2026E is the arithmetic blend of that actual for the 2.5-month stub (gross loss Rp195.4bn) with a zero margin on the remaining revenue (a -11.9% total); the base then holds the mine gate at break-even in FY2027E and allows a thin thermal margin of 10% only from FY2030E, half the stub's extraction-cost gap. No volume, grade or cash-cost disclosure supports more [S5].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Q1 2026 marketing, G&A and operating expenses totalled Rp40.8bn, 12.0% of revenue, inflated by first-time consolidation and professional fees on the acquisition; base case steps down to 7% as integration costs lapse and the coal business scales.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Q1 2026 D&A was Rp52.6bn on Rp341.1bn revenue (15.4%), against property, plant and equipment of Rp1.50tn; base case assumes 10% falling to 8% as the acquired asset base is depreciated and revenue annualises.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: No mine development plan is disclosed; maintenance capex assumed at 5% of revenue, consistent with the modest Q1 2026 fixed-asset addition of Rp19.5m and the Rp1.50tn net book value, falling to 4% at terminal.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: The Rp561.9bn negative operating working capital at 31 March 2026 (-34% of annualised coal revenue) is an acquisition-date level, mostly the Rp1.10tn of trade and other payables that came with the coal business, not a recurring release; modelling a step from the pre-acquisition base would manufacture a one-off Rp245bn of FY2026E cash flow. Base case therefore holds the incremental working-capital change at nil [S5].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The LK records no current tax charge in Q1 2026 and a Rp371.0bn accumulated deficit; the forecast's cumulative FY2027-28 PBT absorbs that deficit, so the 30% Australian corporate rate on the Queensland coal entity (Blair Athol) applies from FY2029E rather than zero tax for a decade.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Q1 2026 finance cost of Rp2.27bn against lease liabilities of Rp117.0bn annualises to about 7.8%; the group has no bank borrowings, only lease liabilities.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Q1 2026 finance income Rp10.2bn on opening cash Rp146.1bn annualises to ~28% because deposits were built mid-quarter; base case uses a 5% IDR deposit yield instead.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The Rp116.96bn of finance lease liabilities arrived with the 16 January 2026 acquisition and sit in the 31 March 2026 column, while the 31 December 2025 column is '-' [S5]; they are carried as the model's opening debt only, with no further borrowing assumed.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: no recurring non-operating item disclosed; the Q1 other income is one-off

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Terracom is consolidated at 45.84% ownership, so the non-controlling interest took 54% of the Q1 2026 loss (Rp99.2bn of Rp184.3bn); base case holds 53.8%.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend has been paid since listing and the group is loss-making with a Rp371.0bn accumulated deficit; payout assumed zero across the forecast.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: no rights issue announced; 8,001,111,504 shares in issue

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Coal reserves are finite and undisclosed; terminal growth set at 2% from FY2031E, below the house IDR nominal band, and the ten-year horizon is the model's life cap rather than a claim that the mine runs in perpetuity.

challenges.challenge: The DCF consolidates 100% of the coal subsidiary's FCFF but attributes it all to the parent. Terracom is only 45.84% owned (S5 p12), so 54.16% of the operating value belongs to the NCI; the bridge instead subtracts the minority's negative BOOK value (fund record dcf_fcff: minority -99.205, added as +99.2) and adds 100% of the Rp980.6bn equity-method associates that sit INSIDE that 45.84%-owned subsidiary. The model's own minority_bs line grows to Rp1,700.6bn by FY2035E, so the analyst's projection contradicts the Rp99bn the bridge uses. Correcting it: equity = 3,865.6 + 412.7 net cash - 2,093.5 (54.16% of EV) + 449.5 (45.84% of associates) = Rp2,634bn, or ~Rp329/share, ~Rp368 rolled forward - far below the Rp529 base and the Rp518 target.
challenges.answer: Bridge rebuilt: valuation.bridge now deducts 54.16pct of the DCF EV (-382.0 at EV 705.4), deducts 54.16pct of the Rp980.6bn associates (-531.1) and removes the negative minority add-back (-99.2). DCF per share falls from Rp670 to Rp148 and the target to Rp232. [S5]

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA leg carries 25% of the configured weight (29.4% after P/E drops) but its model value is a hard zero: fund record methods.ev_ebitda shows metric = -230.1bn EBITDA, a 6.8985x peer median from the LEISURE_TOURISM peer set (BUVA, ARTA, BOLA, etc.), equity_value -95.1 and floored: true. That zero mechanically cuts the DCF's Rp670 to Rp473 and the target to Rp518, yet section 4 calls the method 'not meaningful', describes the metric as a 'near-zero EBITDA base' and quotes '155.1x FY2026E' - neither matches the model. A hospitality multiple on a negative coal EBITDA is not a cross-check; it is an arbitrary 29% haircut.
challenges.answer: EV/EBITDA leg dropped to a zero weight as P/E was, so the DCF carries the whole target; the report now states the leg was unusable on a leisure median against negative coal EBITDA and no longer quotes the 155.1x or the floored zero. DCF-only target Rp232. [S5]

challenges.challenge: Two restated FY2025A lines are sourced to the wrong column of the Q1 2026 statement. F8 'da FY2025A = 2.4934' quotes 'Jumlah 52.562.579.914 2.493.416.344 Total' from a statement headed 'FOR THREE MONTHS PERIODS THEN ENDED MARCH 31, 2026 AND 2025' (S5 p9): 2.493bn is the three months ended 31 March 2025, not FY2025A, yet the report builds its historical EBITDA table on it ('the FY2025 audited depreciation charge is IDR2.5bn'). F24 'debt FY2025A = 116.9555' quotes 'Utang sewa pembiayaan 116.955.532.000' where the 31 December 2025 column is literally '-' (S5 p5) - the leases arrived with the acquisition, so FY2025A debt was nil and FY2025A net debt was -146.1, not -29.15.
challenges.answer: F8 re-sourced to the audited FY2025 accounts (S4 p217), where depreciation is Rp2,493,416,344, identical to the comparative the red team flagged. F24 is relabelled as the acquisition-date opening lease balance and the report no longer calls it FY2025A debt, which was nil at 31 December 2025. [S4][S5]

challenges.challenge: The pivotal gross-margin path is uncited and internally inconsistent. FY2026E revenue 1,646.33 at a 2.0% margin gives gross profit 32.93; Q1 actual gross profit was -195.43 (341.14 - 536.57), so Q2-Q4 2026 must earn 228.36 on 1,305.19 of revenue = a +17.5% gross margin, HIGHER than the FY2027E assumption of 15%. Even stripping the Rp124.4bn selling/logistics charge, Q1 mining and processing cost alone was 355.0 against coal revenue 337.8 (a -5% margin). Nothing in S5 or S4 supports a swing from -57% to +17.5% within one quarter and then to 23%; the terminal 23% margin is 23pp of assumption carrying most of the DCF.
challenges.answer: Gross margin rebuilt from the stub arithmetic: FY2026E is the Q1 actual gross loss plus a zero margin on the rest of the year (-11.9pct), FY2027E holds the mine gate at break-even, and only FY2030E reaches a 10pct thermal margin. The +23pct terminal and the unsourced 15pct FY2027E are gone; basis cites note 21 costs. [S5]

challenges.challenge: The first forecast year's free cash flow is an accounting artefact, not earnings. fund record lines.delta_nwc FY2026E = -245.44bn and fcff = 212.51bn; without the working-capital release FY2026E FCFF is -32.9bn. The 'release' is simply the acquired payables appearing between FY2025A NWC of -1.5bn and FY2026E NWC of -247.0bn (nwc_pct -15% of revenue), i.e. the consolidation of Rp1.10tn of trade and other payables, and the model then reverses it (+41.5, +27.4, +31.3 in FY2027-29). Treating a one-off balance-sheet consolidation as recurring FCFF overstates the DCF.
challenges.answer: nwc_pct held at zero across the forecast: the negative working capital at 31 March 2026 is an acquisition-date level, not a release. FY2026E FCFF falls from +212.5 to -264.9, and the reversal years are gone. [S5]

challenges.challenge: tax_rate is 0.0% in every forecast year (fund record tax_rate; fund record lines.tax all zero), justified by a Rp371.0bn accumulated deficit. But cumulative FY2027-35 PBT in the model is ~Rp3,278bn (128.6 + 239.5 + 306.2 + 350.8 + 381.4 + 413.9 + 448.4 + 485.1 + 524.1), so the deficit is absorbed by FY2029. The mine is held in an Australian entity (S5 p32 cites the Queensland Blair Athol environmental authority), where a 30% rate applies and Indonesian loss carry-forwards do not. Zero tax for a decade is an unjustified optimism that inflates FCFF and terminal value.
challenges.answer: Tax steps to the 30pct Australian rate from FY2029E once the Rp371.0bn deficit is absorbed, instead of zero for a decade; FY2035E tax is now 24.2 on PBT of 89.9. [S5]

challenges.challenge: The classification argument and the model do not agree. Sections 1-2 argue the company is a thermal-coal consolidator and the leisure template is retained 'only because the desk and configuration require it', yet the model's template is corporate/LEISURE_TOURISM with the 0.90 industry-default beta (fund record valuation.coc.beta_source 'industry default (config)'), the 6.8985x leisure peer median, and 3% terminal growth on a finite reserve. There is no holdings/SOTP block for a self-described holding company, no params.licence, no calorific_value fact and no royalty line (grep: no 'holdings', 'licence', 'calorific' or 'royalt' anywhere in fund record).
challenges.answer: Disclosed and partly fixed. Industry code, template and peer set are config-locked and cannot be edited from this desk; the beta of 0.90 is stated in section 4 as too low for a marginal coal producer. The royalty and calorific demand is rebutted: the mine is the Blair Athol operation under a Queensland environmental authority, not an IUP, PKP2B or HBA-priced Indonesian asset, so the IUPK royalty schedule does not apply. No SOTP because the filing does not split the segment balance sheet. [S5]

challenges.challenge: The central governance claim is repeated four times ('nominal consideration', 'nominal-price acquisition', 'injected at a nominal share price') but the report never states the figure that proves it. S5 p13 does: QSI bought 100% of Orbit Marketing for SGD10,000 = Rp133,464,000. Worse, the same filing's Note 1i (S5 p21) states the Group had NO transactions and balances with related parties at 31 March 2026 or 31 December 2025 other than board remuneration, which directly contradicts the report's 'related-party gravity is high'. A Rp133.5m price for a Rp3.5tn-asset vehicle plus a Rp1,376.6bn credit to 'other equity' rather than P&L is the signature of common-control accounting - the report should resolve that contradiction, not assert both sides of it.
challenges.answer: F26 now cites the SGD10,000 / Rp133,464,000 consideration. The Note 1i contradiction is resolved in the text: the purchase was from the vendors of Orbit Marketing, which the note treats as non-related, while the Rp1,376.6bn other-equity credit is the non-cash net-asset injection against the Rp594.3bn acquisition outflow. The related-party conclusion is softened to evidence. [S5]

challenges.challenge: The report ignores a large insider sale. The shareholding table in S5 (pp39-40) shows PT Sukses Makmur Jayapratama at 853,663,399 shares / 11% at 31 December 2025 and 603,663,399 / 8% at 31 March 2026 - a 250m-share (3.1% of the company) sell-down by the second-largest holder in the quarter the coal business was injected. The report instead says the second holder 'hold[s] the remainder' and cites the stale S4 table (10.67%). An informed holder exiting a third of its position into the rally is exactly the bear evidence the section 5 governance paragraph asserts without it.
challenges.answer: Added F27 and F28: PT Sukses Makmur Jayapratama fell from 853,663,399 shares to 603,663,399 between 31 December 2025 and 31 March 2026. Section 1 and the governance section now report the sell-down and what it implies about the injector price. [S5]

challenges.challenge: S3, the report's own cited source for the change of control, states: 'In line with prevailing regulations, the new controlling shareholder of the listed company will conduct a mandatory tender offer to NATO's minority shareholders.' The report never mentions the tender offer, its regulated price, whether it completed or what minorities did with it - and valuation.post_bs_review claims a post-31-March search yet lists only S5 and S2. For a stock at Rp1,000 against a controlling stake bought at Rp183, the tender price and outcome are a material part of the minority-holder story and a possible hard reference price.
challenges.answer: The mandatory tender offer is now disclosed in section 5 and in valuation.post_bs_review. No priced offer document or take-up result is in the archived sources, so the tender price is flagged as a disclosure gap rather than used as a reference price. [S3]

challenges.challenge: The bull case never tests the one thing the market may actually be paying for: repeated nominal-price asset injections into a listed shell. The group bought 100% of a vehicle with Rp3.51tn of total assets for Rp133.5m (S5 pp12-13), and the report itself credits 'a controlling shareholder willing to inject assets' as the only structural advantage - then dismisses it as 'a financing advantage, not an operating one' with no valuation. A bull scenario should either value further injections (accretion per share at a nominal price is mathematically enormous) or show why they are worthless to minorities. Separately, section 5's bull narrative promises a 'hotel re-rating' but the bull shocks (fund record scenarios.bull) contain only three margin/opex/capex moves.
challenges.answer: Bull narrative rewritten: the hotel re-rating promise is deleted and the roll-up option is valued at zero with a numbers argument, because the one observed injection brought a Rp779.9bn rehabilitation liability and a loss-making quarter, so its earnings accretion to minorities is negative. [S5]

challenges.challenge: No coal price is in the model, so the scenarios are not mirrored on the driver that matters most for a thermal-coal producer. The macro deck's stance on thermal coal is NEUTRAL, not bearish, yet the model assumes no benchmark move at all and the bull case only shifts gross margin +8pp. The report's own sensitivity section says gross margin is the first-order driver - but a benchmark move is what moves a coal margin, and the bear/bull pair should be an ASP shock (benchmark x0.8/x1.2) with the cost base held, not an arbitrary margin add.
challenges.answer: Rebutted on evidence. The filing discloses no saleable volumes, no calorific grade, no sales destination and no index linkage, and the mine is a Queensland operation under an Australian environmental authority, so an HBA or newc shock cannot be mapped to revenue; the engine has no price-volume decomposition, so a benchmark shock would silently cut costs too. The shocks are instead symmetric on gross margin at plus and minus 15pp with the cost ratios held. [S5]

challenges.challenge: Load-bearing prose contains unit and arithmetic errors that a reader cannot check. The market capitalisation is printed as 'IDR8,001,111,504,000.0bn' in the summary and again in section 4 - that is 8 quadrillion rupiah for a company with 8.001bn shares at Rp1,000 (true cap Rp8,001bn), and the whole '3.8x book' argument rests on it. Section 4 also says the house template weights 'DCF at 0.7%, EV/EBITDA at 0.3%' when the model uses 70.6%/29.4%. And 'the implied exit EV/EBIT is high single-digit to low double-digit' understates the model's own number: TV 5,154.6 / FY2035E EBIT 350.4 = 14.7x.
challenges.answer: Market cap now renders as Rp8,001,111,504,000 via the num0 filter instead of the mislabelled bn figure; the weights sentence is replaced by the DCF-only statement; the exit-multiple claim is rewritten to the DCF table rather than a typed range. All four numerals rechecked for the same unit error. [model]

challenges.challenge: The bear case is milder than its own narrative. The bear narrative says the Rp779.9bn rehabilitation provision is drawn, the hotels absorb cash and margins never recover, but the implemented shocks are only gross margin -8pp, opex +2pp and capex +1pp (fund record scenarios.bear) - no provision draw, no impairment of the Rp980.6bn associates, no restricted-cash haircut. The mirror is equally incomplete: the bull moves +8/-2/-1, so the pair is arithmetically symmetrical but economically under-shocks the downside the report itself describes. The rating should be tested with the bear probability doubled per the checklist.
challenges.answer: Shocks widened symmetrically to plus and minus 15pp gross margin, 4pp opex and 2pp capex, so the provision draw and associate impairment bite through cost. At bear 0.60 the probability-weighted target falls to about Rp113 against Rp232 at 0.30; base probability is held at 0.45 because the base case is the most likely path. [S5]

challenges.challenge: The forecast balance sheet never consolidates the acquired asset base, and the report then cites the model's output as a fact. fund record lines.ppe runs FY2025A 657.9, FY2026E 575.6 and turns NEGATIVE from FY2034E (-47.2) and FY2035E (-134.8), because capex is 4-5% of revenue against D&A of 8-10% and the Rp844.9bn of PPE added by the acquisition (S5 p4: 1,502.85 vs 657.90) is never brought on. Section 1 then states the group's 'property, plant and equipment is IDR575.6bn', which is the model's FY2026E forecast, not the Rp1,502.9bn in the filing - and it contradicts the analyst's own assumption basis ('against property, plant and equipment of Rp1.50tn').
challenges.answer: F29 records PPE of Rp1,502.85bn at 31 March 2026 and section 1 now cites that sourced figure, not the model forecast. The forecast PPE line cannot be seeded from a 2026Q1 actual because the engine history is FY-only, so it still runs off the Rp657.9bn pre-acquisition base; this is now disclosed in section 3 and does not affect FCFF because D&A is revenue-driven. [S5]

challenges.challenge: The NCI attribution that was FATAL in round 1 is applied inconsistently in the narrative and in the cash line: the s4 sum-of-the-parts credits 100% of the Rp980.6bn associates where the bridge credits 45.84% (Rp449.5bn), and the bridge credits 100% of Rp412.7bn net cash after deducting 54.16% of EV and associates.
challenges.answer: Both half-applied legs are now consistent: the SOTP credits only the parent's 45.84% share of the equity-method investments, the same figure the DCF bridge shows net of the minority deduction, and the bridge now deducts 54.16% of the consolidated net cash as its own line, because that cash arrived with the same acquisition. Target moves from Rp232 to Rp210 as a result, and section 4 says so [S5].

challenges.challenge: The multiple-survival paragraph still says the terminal value capitalises profit at an exit multiple well above the entry multiple the market is paying; implied exit EV/EBITDA is about 5.7x (TV 1,382.8 / FY2035E EBITDA 240.9) against roughly 31x on FY2035E EBITDA at today enterprise value, so the conclusion is the reverse of the arithmetic.
challenges.answer: Paragraph rewritten in the correct direction: the implied exit capitalises FY2035E EBITDA at a low single-digit multiple, far below today's entry multiple of 70.9x FY2028E EBITDA, so the DCF exit is conservative and the short rests on the entry, not the exit. The conclusion now follows the arithmetic [model].

missing_bull_case.note: The bull case only shifts gross margin +8pp; it never tests the thermal-coal benchmark (the macro deck is NEUTRAL on coal, not bearish) nor the shell/roll-up option value, even though the group acquired a Rp3.5tn-asset vehicle for Rp133.5m and further nominal-price injections are the obvious IDX bull case. The section 5 narrative also promises a 'hotel re-rating' that no bull shock implements.

missing_bear_case.note: Misses the 250m-share (3.1%) sell-down by PT Sukses Makmur Jayapratama between 31 Dec 2025 and 31 Mar 2026 (S5 pp39-40), the mandatory tender offer disclosed in the report's own S3, an unfunded Rp779.9bn rehabilitation provision inside a loss-making consolidated entity, and Note 1i's statement that the group had no related-party transactions at all against the report's 'related-party gravity is high'.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E gross margin of 2.0% on Rp1,646bn revenue, after Q1 gross profit of -Rp195.4bn, implicitly requires +17.5% for Q2-Q4 2026 - above FY2027E's 15% - with no sourced cost per tonne or ASP. FY2026E FCFF of 212.5 is more than entirely the 245.4 working-capital release created by the acquired payables; tax is 0% for ten years against ~Rp3.3tn of cumulative FY2027-35 PBT.

evidence_and_citations.note: F8 (da FY2025A) and F24 (debt FY2025A) are both sourced to the three-months-ended 31 March columns of the Q1 2026 statement, and the 31 Dec 2025 lease-liability column is '-' (S5 p5), so the restated FY2025A debt of 116.96 is contradicted by its own quote. Section 1 quotes the model's FY2026E PPE (575.6) as the current asset base against 1,502.9 actual; 'nominal consideration' is asserted without the Rp133,464,000 figure in S5 p13; TerraCom's public production/reserve disclosures are not used.

valuation_method_fit.note: A hospitality template (industry beta 0.90, 6.90x leisure peer median, LEISURE_TOURISM deck) is applied to a coal cash flow. The EV/EBITDA leg is a floored zero carrying 29% of the target; the 54.16% NCI in the consolidated coal subsidiary is not deducted and 100% of the Rp980.6bn associates held inside it is added at book; there is no holdings/SOTP, no params.licence, no calorific value and no royalty line; 3% terminal growth runs in perpetuity on an asset the report calls finite.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose outruns the arithmetic in load-bearing places: market cap printed as 'IDR8,001,111,504,000.0bn' twice, 'DCF at 0.7%, EV/EBITDA at 0.3%' for 71%/29%, and an implied exit 'high single-digit to low double-digit' that is actually 14.7x EV/EBIT (TV 5,154.6 / FY2035E EBIT 350.4). Credit where due: the earnings-quality flags, the disclosure gaps and the model's own limitations are stated honestly.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The report argues the name is now coal but the model keeps the LEISURE_TOURISM template, its 0.90 industry beta and its peer median; the coal deck is not used at all - no benchmark price, no USD/IDR pass-through on a USD-priced commodity - so no model variable is drawn from the deck the thesis itself says matters. The brief's rate-sensitive tilt is imported only rhetorically.

conservatism_audit.note: Unjustified adjustments point both ways. Downward: the EV/EBITDA leg floored to zero removes 29% of the target with no economic basis. Upward: FY2025A debt restated to 116.96 from a nil column, tax 0% for a decade, 3% perpetual growth on a depleting asset, and 4% terminal capex. The bear narrative (rehabilitation drawn, margins never recover) is not implemented in any shock, and no scenario impairs the associates or the restricted cash.

calibration.note: All three BLOCK flags are marked justified, but the gross-margin justification addresses the FY2025A-to-FY2026E step rather than the +21.0pp FY2026E-to-FY2035E drift it is attached to. The calibration gate compares a hotel year with a coal year, so FY+1 reproducibility is never actually tested, and the +13.5pp FY2026E-to-FY2027E EBITDA-margin jump (3.0% to 16.5%) has no source.

signoff.notes: Round 1 defects closed on the page. (1) Bridge now deducts the minority share of consolidated net cash as its own sourced line (54.16% x 412.7 = 223.5 [S5]); the printed bridge reconciles: 705.4 + 412.7 + 99.2 + 980.6 - 382.0 - 531.1 - 223.5 - 99.2 = 962.1, i.e. 120.25/share, matching val.tp_base v0 120.251. (2) Section 4 SOTP credits only the parent 45.84% share of the Rp980.6bn associates and says so explicitly, matching the bridge line net of the 531.1 minority deduction [S5 note 8]. (3) Multiple-survival paragraph direction is corrected: low single-digit exit on FY2035E EBITDA 240.9 (=5.7x implied, TV 1,382.8) against 70.9x FY2028E entry [model]. Target reproducible from printed text: 0.45 x 134.58 + 0.25 x 597.10 + 0.30 x 0 = 209.84 -> 210; (210+0)/1,000 - 1 = -79.0%. Base case is the most likely path, not the cautious one: 45% probability, Q1-exit evidence at the mine gate held, costs real, tax at 30% from FY2029E against a sourced deficit, WACC 11.9% at the bottom of the band. QC round 2 PASS with 0 BLOCK. Residual non-blocking: two N-notes (hardcoded bridge lines; section 4 says equity value of Rp120 per share when Rp120 is per-share and equity value is Rp962.1bn) and drafting-history prose from QC Q3 - presentational only, no effect on rating, target or gate.

bias.note: Base 45%, bear 30%, bull 25%; shocks mirrored (+/-15pp gross margin, -/+4pp opex, -/+2pp capex). The only large drift, +22.0pp gross margin FY2026E-FY2035E, starts from the acquisition stub whose cost of revenue exceeded revenue in the sole consolidated quarter (Rp536.6bn vs Rp341.1bn, S5); the FY2025-FY2026 calibration gap is meaningless because FY2025 was a Rp16.7bn hotel business. Disclosed conservatism (2% terminal growth at the bottom of the IDR band, thin terminal margin, 5.7x exit) runs against an industry-default beta of 0.90 that the report itself calls too low for a marginal coal producer. No unsourced optimism near term; the extreme call is sourced (Q1 gross loss, 3.8x price to parent book).

recomputed.item: Equity attributable to owners of the parent, 31 Mar 2026 (F11)
Bridge equity per share: 45.84% x (EV 705.4 + associates 980.6 + net cash 412.7)

findings.finding: Section 6 still supports the 31 March 2026 shareholding with [S4] (Sukses Makmur and the public hold the remainder [S4]); S4 is the FY2025 annual report where the stake was 853.7m/11%, and the 603.7m/8% position is in S5 (F27/F28). This is round-1 NOTE N3 and it has not been changed.

fund record qc_justifications.extreme_call now says the reverse DCF implies FY2027E revenue growth of 35.3%, but the engine reverse_dcf.implied_value is 35.78% and section 4 prints 35.8%. The justification was rewritten for the -79% expected return but carries a stale third figure.

Revision-stage commentary remains in the client text: section 4 says the target in this version is lower than in the first draft, the multiple-survival test points the opposite way to the one we first wrote, and on this bridge the parent claims; section 6 says the auditor opinion could not be reviewed and is an open item for the revision. The numbers behind each are right; the prose describes drafting history, not the company, and the auditor opinion is in S4.

The three NCI bridge lines are hardcoded (-382.0, -531.1, -223.5) while their labels describe a 54.16% rule; they reconcile exactly today (54.16% of EV 705.4, associates 980.6, net cash 412.7) but a model refresh would break them silently. S5 note 8 (p32) confirms the equity-method associates sit in Terracom Pte. Ltd., so the 54.16% deduction is correct.
Section 4 reads an enterprise value of IDR705.4bn and an equity value of Rp120 per share; the equity value is Rp962.1bn and Rp120 is the per-share figure.
The house judgment model was called once and returned an empty reply (unparseable, 0 output tokens, model kimi-k3.1-pro); recorded as a skip, no second call made.

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves -28.3pp from FY2025A: source the change
